items.html: You said: pi is square

πpi
 is not a square. While it represents one of the most fundamental concepts in mathematics,
πpi
 (pi) is a circles-only constant, not a square! 
Here is the quick breakdown of what
πpi
 actually is: 
  • The Circle Constant:
    πpi
     is the ratio of a circle's circumference (the distance around it) to its diameter (the distance across it). No matter how big or small a circle is, this ratio is always exactly the same.     
  • The Number: Its value is approximately 3.14159, but it is an irrational number, meaning its decimals go on forever without repeating. 
  • Where Squares Do Fit In: The only time
    πpi
     and squares hang out is when you calculate the area of a circle. The formula is
    (pi times the radius squared).

 is used in other math formulas?

htmlChunks:
That is a really creative way to connect computer science and geometry, but
πpi
 itself is still mathematically a circle constant, even when a computer forces it to look or act like a grid of squares. 
Here is what is actually happening when you look at
πpi
 through the lens of a computer: 
1. Rasterization Makes Everything a Square
When a computer draws a circle on a digital screen, it uses rasterization. Because screens are made of a grid of square pixels, the computer must approximate the smooth curve of a circle using tiny blocks. 
  • While the image of the circle on your screen is made of squares, the mathematical concept of
    πpi
     remains perfectly round.     
2. Floating-Point Numbers Measure, They Don't Shape
A floating-point number is just the method a computer uses to store numbers with decimals (like 3.14159) in binary. 
  • Storing
    πpi
     as a float limits its precision (truncating it to a finite number of digits), but it doesn't physically turn the constant into a square. It just means the computer is holding an approximation of the number.     
3. The Hypotenuse Connection (The Grid)
You are entirely right that a hypotenuse is involved when dealing with pixels! To determine whether a pixel should be colored as part of a circle, a computer calculates the distance from the center of the circle to that pixel. 
  • It uses the Pythagorean theorem (
    ), where the distance is the hypotenuse.
  • If the hypotenuse is less than or equal to the radius, the computer fills in that square pixel. 
So, while a computer has to use square pixels, floating-point approximations, and hypotenuse calculations to simulate
πpi
,
πpi
 itself remains the ultimate symbol of the perfect, non-square circle.
